NPM PROVENANCE CHECK · ONE READ-ONLY REQUEST PER PACKAGE

Which of your dependencies lack a provenance attestation?

Paste a package-lock.json, a package.json, or a plain list of package names, and see which ones were published with an npm provenance attestation -- trusted publishing (OIDC, no long-lived token to steal) or npm publish --provenance from a supported CI -- and which still rely on a classic publish token, the exact mechanism the 2025-2026 Shai-Hulud worm abused to compromise maintainer accounts and push malicious versions.

Your file is parsed in this browser and never uploaded. Checking a package makes one GET request, from your browser, to the public npm registry -- the same one npm install already talks to.

1. Paste a lockfile, package.json, or a plain list

2. Provenance by package

PackageVersion checkedProvenanceDetail

Prefer a CLI, or want this in CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

node cli.mjs package-lock.json
node cli.mjs package-lock.json --json
node cli.mjs package-lock.json --without-provenance-only
node cli.mjs package.json                      # unpinned: checks the latest published version
echo "vite\nleft-pad@1.3.0" | node cli.mjs -    # freeform list on stdin

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. Reads only the file you name; the only network calls are the per-package registry lookups.

Common questions

Why isn't npm audit signatures enough?

npm audit signatures reports provenance too, but only for the packages already installed in the project you currently have open, one project at a time, with no report you can hand to a teammate or wire into a dashboard across several repos. This tool works from a pasted lockfile, package.json, or plain list -- no install required -- and the CLI emits JSON for scripting. More: why this exists alongside npm audit signatures.

Does a package without provenance mean it's compromised?

No. Most published npm packages predate trusted publishing (general availability was July 2025) or their maintainer hasn't migrated yet -- popular, actively maintained packages show up with no provenance attestation too. The absence of provenance is a fact about how a version was published, not a verdict on whether it is safe.

Is my package-lock.json uploaded anywhere?

No. The file is parsed entirely in your browser. What does leave your browser is one read-only GET request per package name/version to registry.npmjs.org, the same public registry npm install already talks to.

What counts as a provenance attestation?

The registry's own per-version metadata carries a dist.attestations.provenance field when that version was published via trusted publishing or npm publish --provenance from a supported CI. This tool reports exactly that field.

How is this different from a supply-chain security platform like Socket?

Different layers. Socket watches a connected dependency graph and the public registries on an ongoing basis across dozens of risk categories. This tool answers one narrower, one-time question from a pasted lockfile or the CLI: does this exact package version carry the registry's own provenance field? See this checker vs. Socket.

Been checking packages one at a time on npmjs.com? See this checker vs. checking each package on npmjs.com by hand.

Everything runs in your browser. The file you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Also worth a pass over the same dependency tree: npm Lifecycle Script Check lists every package that runs an install-time script, Lockfile License Check lists every dependency licence and flags GPL, AGPL and unlicensed packages, and Slopsquatting Check flags a dependency name that looks like a hallucinated or freshly squatted look-alike before it resolves to a malicious package. Got a Python dependency tree too? PyPI Provenance Check reports the same trusted-publishing signal for PyPI packages.

vs-checking-each-package-on-npmjs-by-han.text:
← npm Provenance Check

npm Provenance Check vs. checking each package on npmjs.com by hand

Opening one package's npmjs.com page and checking its provenance badge works fine for a single dependency you're curious about. It does not scale to a package-lock.json with dozens or hundreds of packages, each needing the right resolved version's page found, checked, and the result written down — which is what this free, no-upload checker does in one pass from a pasted file.

Where checking it yourself stops being enough

Anyone curious about one specific dependency already does this: open its page on npmjs.com, switch to the version you actually have installed, and look for the provenance badge. For a single package that's a minute of clicking. The problem is a real dependency tree is rarely one package — it's a package-lock.json with dozens of direct and transitive entries, and the manual version of this check does not get easier per-package as the list grows.

What you're trying to confirmChecking npmjs.com yourselfThis checker
Whether one specific package's page shows a provenance badge.Works. This is the one case a single manual lookup reliably handles.Also handles it, in the same pass as every other package in your file.
Finding the exact version your lockfile resolved — not just whatever npmjs.com shows by default — among however many versions that project has published.Requires switching the version dropdown to match your lockfile's resolved version, for every package.Reads the resolved version straight out of the pasted package-lock.json, the same way every time.
Doing the same lookup consistently across a lockfile with dozens or hundreds of direct and transitive dependencies.The same several clicks repeated over and over, with no running tally except what you remember or type into a separate note; easy to drop a row partway through.Every package in the pasted file, checked the same mechanical way, with nothing skipped.
Producing a list of just the packages still missing an attestation, in a form you can hand to a teammate or feed to a migration tracker.Nothing beyond whatever you wrote down yourself while clicking through pages.The CLI emits exactly that list as JSON in one run.
Re-checking the whole dependency tree again after package-lock.json changes.The full manual pass again, one package at a time.One paste, the whole file, every time.

A quick look at one package's page is still the fastest way to answer a one-off question, and this checker isn't reading anything npmjs.com doesn't already publish — it's reading the same dist.attestations.provenance registry field a manual check would eventually reach, just resolving every package in a pasted file automatically instead of leaving the lookup to be repeated by hand across however many dependencies the lockfile has.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: your file is parsed entirely in your browser, and only package names and versions ever leave it, in read-only requests to the public npm registry.

Common questions

Can't I just look up each package on npmjs.com myself?

For one package, yes -- open its npmjs.com page, find the version you actually installed, and check whether that version's page shows a provenance badge. What doesn't scale is doing that for every package in a package-lock.json: each one needs its own page found, the specific resolved version located among however many versions that project has published, and the result written down somewhere before you move to the next package. This tool resolves and checks every package in a pasted file in one pass.

Why is matching the right resolved version easy to get wrong by hand?

A package-lock.json records the exact resolved version npm installed for every direct and transitive dependency, but npmjs.com's package page shows the badge for whichever version you land on -- by default the latest, not necessarily the one your lockfile pins. Finding the one version page that matches what your lockfile actually resolved, for every package in the file, is the kind of lookup that is reliable when a tool does it the same way every time and error-prone when it depends on remembering to change the version dropdown before reading the badge.

Why is it easy to lose track partway through a long dependency list?

A typical project's package-lock.json runs to dozens or hundreds of direct and transitive dependencies. Checking each one by hand means repeating the same several clicks -- find the package, switch to the resolved version, look for the provenance badge, note the result -- over and over, with no running tally except what you remember or type into a separate note. It is the same kind of repetitive, easy-to-drop-a-row task a mechanical pass through a pasted lockfile does exactly the same way every time.

What do I get from a manual check that this tool doesn't produce?

Nothing extra -- both read the same registry facts. What a manual pass through npmjs.com doesn't produce on its own is a single list of which packages in your file lack an attestation, in a form you can hand to a teammate, paste into a migration tracker, or feed to another script. This tool's CLI emits that list as JSON in one run; a manual check produces only whatever you wrote down yourself.

Is this page making a live comparison against a tool or company?

No. This page describes a manual habit any maintainer or reviewer already has -- opening a package's npmjs.com page and checking its provenance badge before trusting it. It names no competing product or company. This tool makes only read-only requests to the public npm registry, the same facts a manual page visit would show.

← npm Provenance Check

This checker vs. Socket

Two different layers: Socket watches a connected dependency graph and the public registries on an ongoing basis across 70+ risk categories. This tool answers one narrower, one-time question from a pasted lockfile or the CLI — does this exact package version carry npm's own dist.attestations.provenance field — with no account and nothing installed.

What each product is for

Socket is a supply-chain security platform. Its own site describes deep package inspection that characterizes what a dependency actually does, connected through a GitHub app, a CLI, or a browser extension, and it flags more than 70 categories of risk across npm and other ecosystems — malware, typosquatting, hidden or obfuscated code, and permission creep among them — while monitoring a project's dependency graph on an ongoing basis. It is free for public, open-source use, and Socket's own site lists paid Team, Business, and Enterprise tiers for private-repository and organization use. Socket has written publicly about npm provenance and trusted publishing, so provenance is plausibly one signal folded into its broader per-package score for a connected project; this page does not claim to know exactly how Socket weighs or surfaces it, since this session cannot verify that live against Socket's own product.

This tool does none of what Socket does. It has no account, no ongoing service, no GitHub app, and it never scores a package or a project. Given a pasted package-lock.json, package.json, or a plain list of package names, it makes one read-only GET request per package to registry.npmjs.org — the same registry npm install already talks to — and reports exactly the dist.attestations.provenance field the registry publishes for that version: present (published via trusted publishing/OIDC or npm publish --provenance) or absent (a classic, stealable long-lived token). Nothing is uploaded, nothing is connected, and nothing is remembered between runs beyond what you paste again next time.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want continuous, registry-aware scanning of my whole dependency graph for malware, typosquats, permission creep, and dozens of other supply-chain risks — not just publish provenance.Socket — that is the ongoing, cross-ecosystem job it is built for.
I want to know right now, for free, exactly which packages in a pasted lockfile lack a provenance attestation, with no account and nothing connected.This tool — paste it, get the list, nothing installed.
I want a GitHub app or CLI that watches every future pull request for newly introduced supply-chain risk.Socket — this tool has no memory between runs and watches nothing on its own.
I want a single, exportable report across several repositories' lockfiles with no sign-up, wired into a script with --json.This tool's CLI — paste or point it at each lockfile in turn.
I want to know whether a specific package has ever shown malicious behavior, or is a typosquat of a popular name.Socket — this tool checks one registry field and cannot answer that.
I want the exact registry-documented provenance field, per package version, with no interpretation or score layered on top.This tool — that is the one fact it reports, nothing more.

A team can reasonably run both: Socket for continuous, registry-aware defense against a live attack already under way, and this tool as a fast, zero-account, zero-install check of exactly which dependencies still publish through a stealable token — useful on its own, or before deciding whether Socket's broader connected monitoring is worth setting up at all. This page does not evaluate Socket's detection accuracy or how it weighs provenance and makes no claim about either — it only describes Socket's documented product shape and states what this tool does differently. A clean result from either one is not a guarantee that a dependency is safe: absence of a provenance attestation is a fact about how a version was published, not a verdict.

why-not-just-npm-audit-signatures.html.text:
← back to npm Provenance Check

Why not just npm audit signatures?

The npm CLI already has a command that reports provenance:

npm audit signatures

It's real, it's accurate, and if all you want is a one-time answer for the project in front of you, it's the right tool -- this page isn't arguing against it. What it doesn't do is what this tool exists for.

Three gaps this tool fills

1. It needs a full install of the project. npm audit signatures reads your local node_modules and package-lock.json, which means npm install has already run. This tool works from a pasted lockfile, package.json, or even a plain list of names -- useful when you're evaluating a dependency before adding it, reviewing someone else's lockfile they sent you, or checking a repo you haven't cloned.

2. It's one project at a time, with no report to hand off. If you maintain (or audit) more than one repository, there's no built-in way to see "which of these 40 repos still has unmigrated dependencies" without running the command in each one and copying results by hand. This tool's CLI emits --json, so a script can loop over repos and diff the output.

3. No bulk or CI-shaped output. npm audit signatures is built for a human reading a terminal, not for a machine reading a report. The CLI here has a flag built for exactly that:

node cli.mjs package-lock.json --without-provenance-only --json

which returns just the packages still missing an attestation, as JSON, ready to file into a spreadsheet, a Slack digest, or a migration tracker.

What both tools read is the same fact

There is no separate provenance database. Both npm audit signatures and this tool read the same registry field -- dist.attestations.provenance on a published version -- so they will never disagree about a given package's status. The difference is entirely in what you can start from and what you get out, not in what's being measured.

Common questions

Does npm audit signatures already do this?

Yes -- npm audit signatures reports the same registry provenance field this tool does. What it does not do is work from a lockfile before you have installed the project, produce a report across more than one repository, or emit JSON another tool can consume. Those three gaps are what this tool adds.

Do npm audit signatures and this tool ever disagree?

No. Both read the exact same registry field, dist.attestations.provenance, on the exact same published version. There is no separate provenance database for either tool to disagree about.

When should I use npm audit signatures instead?

When you already have the project installed locally and only need a one-time answer for that one project -- it needs no separate tool and no network request beyond what npm already made during install.
